title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
hook: a rope, a hook, a sugarcane bow and flower arrows: what the goddess holds, and what the hymn says they are

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama began: the goddess born from the fire-altar of consciousness, risen ready for the work of the gods. Today, her hands.
screen: `BORN FROM THE FIRE OF CONSCIOUSNESS.` → `READY FOR THE WORK.`

segments.voice: A rope. A hook for steering an elephant. A bow cut from sugarcane. Arrows tipped with flowers. That's what the goddess Lalita holds in her four hands, in paintings and temple images. An odd inventory: a noose and a goad sound like tools for catching and driving animals, and a sugarcane bow sounds like something out of a children's story. But the Lalita Sahasranama doesn't leave the objects as objects. A short run of names, early in the hymn, says what each one really is.
screen: `A ROPE, A HOOK, A BOW, ARROWS.` → `AN ODD INVENTORY.` → `FOUR NAMES FOR FOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: After the names of her rising from a fire of consciousness, the hymn describes her form, and four names in a row say what she carries. In paraphrase: she holds the noose that is desire. The Sanskrit there is raga: passion, attachment, the pull toward what we want. She shines with the goad that is anger, the hooked stick that keeps an elephant moving or turns it aside. Her bow of sugarcane is the mind. And her arrows are the five subtle elements, the tanmatras, the subtle forms of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, what the senses meet. Desire, anger, the mind, the senses. The Bhagavad Gita traces how dwelling on things breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger. These are the hard parts of an inner life, and in this hymn they aren't thrown away or trampled. They're in the goddess's hands. Readers take that more than one way. Some say she holds them, so they have no hold on her: the rope that binds a person is, for her, a tool. Others hear something gentler: even a person's desire and anger are not outside her reach. And some notice the sweetness. The mind is a bow, but a bow of sugarcane, and its arrows are flowers. In the old stories Kama, the god of love, carries a sugarcane bow and flower arrows too; the path will come back to him. For today, just the picture: what looks like a rack of weapons turns out to be the inner life, held steady.
screen: `THE NOOSE IS DESIRE.` · `THE GOAD IS ANGER.` · `THE BOW IS THE MIND, THE ARROWS THE SENSES.` · `HELD, NOT THROWN AWAY.` · then, large: `THE INNER LIFE, HELD STEADY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small want you're carrying today and notice it the way you'd notice a rope in someone's hand: there, held; then one irritation, then the busy mind, then one sound or touch, each seen the same way. Nothing to fix. If you pray, you can offer each to the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let them rest in open hands.
The Lalita Sahasranama. The hymn of names for the goddess Lalita, and today four of them: the noose, the goad, the bow and the arrows.
Your line: the Lalita Sahasranama, in selections. A want can be something held, rather than something holding you. Day one thousand one hundred two, done.

howItsDone: Devotees of the goddess recite the Lalita Sahasranama at home or in temples, and images of Lalita show her four-armed, holding the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow and the flower arrows the hymn describes.

notes: Names paraphrased: 4 cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā (born from the fire-pit of consciousness), 7 caturbāhusamanvitā (four-armed), 8 rāgasvarūpapāśāḍhyā (holding the noose whose form is desire), 9 krodhākārāṅkuśojjvalā (shining with the goad whose form is anger), 10 manorūpekṣukodaṇḍā (whose sugarcane bow is the mind), 11 pañcatanmātrasāyakā (whose arrows are the five tanmātras). Confirm numbering and glosses.
Glossing the tanmātras as 'the subtle forms of sound, touch, form, taste and smell' is a simplification; confirm.

The three readings (she holds them so they don't hold her; a person's passions are within her reach; the sweetness of the bow) are attributed to commentators and 'some readers' without naming a commentary. Bhaskararaya's Saubhagya Bhaskara may support the first; confirm before attributing to him by name.
Kama's sugarcane bow and flower arrows: standard iconography; tomorrow's story (Kama burned and revived) picks this up.
Gita 2.62–63 paraphrased (dwelling on objects, attachment, desire, anger).
